title: Investigating ESL Learners’ Perception and Problem towards Artificial Intelligence (AI) -Assisted English Language Learning and Teaching
extended_summary:
This paper examines how ESL learners perceive artificial intelligence-assisted English language learning and what problems they encounter when using AI-powered tools for language study. The study is motivated by the growing use of AI applications in education, especially in Education 4.0 and language learning contexts, and seeks to understand both the perceived benefits and practical barriers of AI-assisted English learning.

The researchers used a quantitative descriptive survey design. A 5-point Likert-scale questionnaire was distributed through Google Forms to second-year engineering students, focusing on two areas: perceptions of AI-assisted English learning and problems associated with using AI-powered applications. The study did not test a specific single AI intervention; rather, it investigated students’ experiences with a range of AI-powered applications such as robots, voice assistants, chatbots, speech recognition, and related tools used for academic purposes.

The participants were 81 respondents from an initial group of 130 second-year engineering students enrolled in a Technical Report Writing course at Vellore Institute of Technology in southern India. These students were from various engineering streams and were already exposed to different technological tools, including AI applications. Data were analyzed mainly using mean scores, standard deviations, and reliability checks via Cronbach’s alpha in SPSS.

The study found that students generally held favorable perceptions of AI-assisted English language learning, with the strongest perceived benefits being time savings and the ability to learn anywhere and anytime. At the same time, students reported substantial barriers, especially the lack of good-quality AI language-learning apps on smartphones, insufficient app features for English learning, and cost-related concerns. The authors conclude that AI-powered tools have promise as instructional media for ESL learning, but current applications require improvement—especially in quality and NLP support—and they recommend further experimental and broader-based research on AI use in language learning classrooms.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic AI-powered applications for English language learning and teaching, including voice assistants, chatbots, speech recognition, and other AI-assisted language learning tools, with no single focal product evaluated.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed ESL engineering students' perceptions of and problems with using AI-powered applications for English language learning and teaching.

findings.finding_summary: Students reported favorable perceptions toward AI-assisted English language learning overall (mean=4.058 on a 5-point Likert scale; n=81). The highest-rated perceived benefits were that AI-powered applications save time (mean=4.22, SD=0.758) and allow learning English anywhere, anytime (mean=4.22, SD=0.742).
findings.measure: Student perception survey on AI-assisted English language learning (5-point Likert scale means and SDs)

findings.finding_summary: Learners identified substantial implementation problems with AI-assisted English learning overall (mean=3.580 on a 5-point Likert scale; n=81). The most prominent reported barrier was that smartphones do not have good AI apps for language learning (mean=4.33, SD=0.822), followed by the view that AI app characteristics do not support English learning well (mean=4.02, SD=0.866).
findings.measure: Student problem survey on AI-assisted English language learning (5-point Likert scale means and SDs)

quality_tier_rationale: This is a quantitative descriptive survey study of student perceptions and barriers, not an experimental or quasi-experimental evaluation of learning effects. The methodology is clear, but evidence is self-reported and correlational/descriptive.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports favorable perceptions and notable barriers, but no causal effect sizes or objective learning gains are provided. Impact on student outcomes is therefore unclear.
